configuration.content:
A while ago, I built a minimal CMS for a statically hosted personal website. The idea was to see how far I could take a configurable website without paying for a server or maintaining a backend.

It was a fairly simple implementation. It worked, but I eventually left it unattended.

Recently, I decided to revisit that idea. I had accumulated more experience since the first attempt, and I wanted to address some of the architectural limitations I had encountered.

This time, I wanted something more complete: a portfolio that could be forked, configured entirely through a browser-based interface, and deployed without requiring its owner to understand the underlying codebase.

The result is portfolio.

It is built with Next.js and deployed as a static website through GitHub Pages. GitHub is the content storage backend; the GitHub Contents API handles reads and writes, and GitHub Actions orchestrates configuration migrations, asset processing, and deployment.

There is no custom backend server, database, or separately hosted authentication service.

Here's how the system works and some of the engineering decisions behind it.

1. GitHub as a Content Backend

The central idea is simple: why introduce a database and a server when the content can live directly in a Git repository?

The website's configuration is stored as JSON files in the repository. Instead of asking users to edit those files manually, I built a browser-based setup interface that manages them.

The editing workflow looks like this:

  1. Open the /setup section of the deployed website.

  2. Authenticate using a GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT).

  3. Select the repository to manage.

  4. Edit website content, configuration, appearance, and other information through the UI.

  5. Save the changes.

Behind the scenes, the browser communicates directly with the GitHub Contents API.

When saving configuration, the application validates the data against its corresponding Zod schema, serializes it into a versioned JSON structure, encodes it, and commits the changes to the repository through GitHub's API.

GitHub Actions then takes over the build and deployment process.

The important distinction is that the public-facing website does not need to make runtime API requests to retrieve its content. The configuration is read during the build, and the resulting website is exported as static assets.

The setup interface is part of the same application, but it is not part of the public content experience.

This gives me two distinct experiences within one application:

  • A static, publicly accessible website.

  • A browser-based content management interface that writes directly to the repository.

The setup route is also disallowed in robots.txt to discourage search engine indexing. It is not a security boundary; access to editing operations still depends on GitHub authentication.

The motivation behind this architecture was to eliminate infrastructure that a personal website doesn't necessarily need.

For an individual maintaining their own portfolio, GitHub can provide content storage, version history, and an API without requiring another service to operate.

2. Configuration Architecture and Schema Validation

My earlier implementation had one large configuration file. Everything was stored together.

That became increasingly difficult to maintain as the website grew.

In this version, configuration is divided into independent sections. About, projects, skills, journey, gallery, testimonials, blogs, services, and other sections each have their own configuration file and corresponding schema.

This separation provides a much cleaner boundary between different parts of the website.

I use Zod for configuration schemas. Beyond runtime validation, the schemas serve two additional purposes:

  • TypeScript types are inferred directly from the schemas, avoiding independently maintained type definitions.

  • Schema metadata provides the information needed to construct the configuration editing interface.

Adding a new configurable section still involves a few deliberate steps. I define its Zod schema, use that schema to construct the data model and derive its TypeScript types, integrate the resulting data into the relevant UI, and build the corresponding editing form in the setup panel so the configuration can be modified and saved.

I designed a set of reusable components and utilities to make this process faster and reduce repetitive implementation work. The schema provides a consistent foundation for validation and type inference, while the shared components handle much of the recurring form and configuration-editing logic. This doesn't eliminate the work of integrating a new section, but it makes the process more predictable and considerably less repetitive.

3. Versioned Configurations and Automatic Migrations

Once configuration is separated into multiple files, another problem becomes important: configurations evolve.

Suppose someone forks the project today and customizes their portfolio. A few months later, I introduce a new field or change the structure of an existing configuration.

What happens to their existing data?

I didn't want every update to require users to manually modify JSON files or recreate their configurations.

Each configuration is therefore stored inside a versioned envelope:

{
  "version": 1,
  "configuration": {
    "summary": "..."
  }
}

The migration manager maintains the current version of each configuration type and a registry of migration functions.

When a configuration is loaded, the migration manager determines its current version and executes the required migrations sequentially until it reaches the version expected by the application.

For example, if a configuration needs to move from version 0 to version 2, the migration manager executes the version 1 migration followed by the version 2 migration.

Each migration is responsible for one transition.

This makes changes such as renaming properties, restructuring data, or introducing new fields manageable without requiring users to manually update their existing configurations.

I also integrated this into the CI pipeline.

When a fork receives changes, a GitHub Actions workflow installs the project dependencies, runs the migration script, commits any migrated configurations, and triggers deployment.

Configuration evolution becomes part of the application's update process rather than an additional maintenance task for its users.

4. Fork Synchronization Without Losing Customizations

Making a project forkable is relatively easy. Keeping those forks up to date without overwriting user customizations is a different problem.

I wanted users to be able to fork the repository, customize their websites, and still benefit from future improvements to the original project.

The synchronization workflow periodically checks the upstream repository for changes and merges them into the fork.

However, there is an important distinction between application code and user configuration.

The application should receive upstream improvements. The user's personal content should remain theirs.

To handle this, the workflow merges upstream changes and explicitly restores the fork's own public/config directory from its original branch before pushing the synchronized result.

If there are upstream changes, the configuration migration workflow runs afterward.

This creates a relatively straightforward update cycle:

  1. Synchronize application changes from upstream.

  2. Preserve the fork's own configuration.

  3. Migrate outdated configuration structures.

  4. Build and deploy the updated website.

The idea is to make the repository behave more like an independently customizable application that can still receive upstream maintenance.

There are limitations to this approach, particularly around conflicting modifications to application code, but it removes a significant amount of manual work from keeping a fork current.

5. Rich-Text Editing and Content Management

A portfolio shouldn't require its owner to understand HTML or manually edit structured content.

For blogs and other rich-text sections, I integrated a block editor built on TipTap.

The editor provides a visual writing experience with block-level editing, formatting, and other rich-text capabilities.

Blog content is also separated from blog metadata.

The main blog configuration maintains information such as:

  • Post ID

  • Title and summary

  • Publication date

  • Categories and tags

  • Accent color

  • Current and historical URL slugs

The actual rich-text content is stored separately in files associated with the post's stable ID.

This separation keeps the main configuration manageable while allowing individual posts to contain substantially richer content.

It also makes it easier to evolve blog metadata independently of the content itself.

6. Preserving URLs Through Slug History

One problem with static websites is that changing a URL can break existing links.

For example, consider a blog post initially published at:

/blogs/getting-started-with-nextjs/

Later, I decide to rename it and generate a new slug:

/blogs/building-with-nextjs/

Simply replacing the old slug would break existing links.

Instead, the application maintains a history of slugs for each content item.

Each slug has an isActive property. When a title changes, the previous slug becomes historical, and the new slug becomes active.

During the build, both active and historical slugs are included in the static route parameters.

Consequently, the old URL continues to resolve to the same content without requiring server-side redirect handling.

The slug generation logic also tracks previously used slugs to prevent collisions.

This approach is applied to content types that use slug-based routing, including blog posts, projects, and gallery categories.

It is a small architectural decision, but one that makes a static website considerably more resilient to content changes.

7. Image Processing as a CI Responsibility

Image processing is another task that commonly requires server-side infrastructure.

I moved this responsibility into GitHub Actions.

Whenever images are added or changed under public/uploads/, a workflow processes them using Python and Pillow.

It generates thumbnails with a maximum dimension of 640 × 640 pixels, using Lanczos resampling.

For JPEG and WebP images, it also applies optimization settings.

The workflow maintains the thumbnail directory alongside the original uploads and removes thumbnails whose corresponding source files no longer exist.

It also runs periodically, allowing the generated assets to be reconciled even if a previous workflow run was interrupted.

The result is that image processing happens during the repository's automation cycle, not through a separately hosted image-processing service.

8. Client-Side Search Without a Search Service

The website also includes search functionality across content such as projects, skills, and milestones.

Rather than introducing a separate search service, I implemented a small client-side fuzzy-search utility.

It normalizes text, handles differences in capitalization and punctuation, and ranks results using several matching strategies.

These include exact matches, prefix matches, substring matches, and edit-distance-based comparisons.

The implementation also accounts for transposed characters.

This provides more forgiving search behavior without requiring a backend search index or an additional runtime dependency.

For the relatively small datasets typical of a personal portfolio, client-side search is sufficient.

9. The Build and Deployment Pipeline

The automation is what brings the architecture together.

There are separate GitHub Actions workflows responsible for different parts of the system:

Fork synchronization

Checks for upstream changes, merges application updates, and preserves local configuration.

Configuration migration

Runs the migration script against existing configuration files, commits changes when necessary, and triggers deployment.

Static deployment

Builds the Next.js application using static export and publishes the generated output through GitHub Pages.

Thumbnail generation

Processes uploaded images, generates optimized thumbnails, and removes orphaned assets.

These workflows are connected through GitHub Actions workflow dispatch events where one stage needs to trigger another.

The Next.js application uses output: 'export', producing a static deployment rather than relying on a Next.js server at runtime.

The deployment workflow also configures the site's base path and canonical URL based on the GitHub Pages environment.

This allows the same project to work with GitHub Pages URLs as well as custom domains, without manually changing the application's routing and SEO configuration.

10. SEO and Metadata

A portfolio is also a public representation of its owner, so discoverability matters.

I centralized page metadata generation instead of maintaining separate metadata logic throughout the application.

The metadata utility handles:

  • Page titles and descriptions.

  • Canonical URLs.

  • Open Graph metadata.

  • Twitter card metadata.

  • Author information.

  • Keywords.

  • Article-specific metadata.

  • Robots directives.

It also generates metadata using the site's configured identity and URL.

The application includes a sitemap and a robots.txt endpoint, with the sitemap URL generated from the configured canonical domain.

The intention is to make SEO configuration part of the website's content and build process rather than something that needs to be maintained independently for every page.

11. How the Project Evolved

One aspect I find particularly interesting about this project is how it developed.

The current implementation wasn't designed in one sitting.

It started with an earlier project, personal-website-cms-source, which tested the original idea of managing a statically hosted website through a browser.

That implementation used a monolithic configuration file and had a much more limited editing experience.

When I revisited the idea, I wanted to address several things:

  • Separate configuration files instead of maintaining one large configuration.

  • Eliminate runtime API dependencies from public-facing pages.

  • Introduce configuration versioning and migrations.

  • Make the setup interface a proper content management experience.

  • Establish a reliable deployment and fork synchronization process.

  • Introduce explicit relationships between related content rather than relying on duplicated text.

I built the configuration models and hooks, developed the different website sections, reconsidered the UI implementation, and eventually moved toward shadcn/ui.

The migration system followed the introduction of configuration versioning. Local configuration support came from the need to experiment without committing every development change. Fork synchronization came from the requirement that the project should be maintainable as a reusable template.

There was plenty of iteration along the way.

Some decisions were made because a previous implementation became inconvenient. Others came from realizing that a feature would become difficult to maintain if I didn't establish a better structure early enough.

I think that is an important part of software development that is often missing from project write-ups.

Not every useful architectural decision comes from anticipating every possible requirement. Sometimes it comes from building something, understanding its limitations, and improving the design as those limitations become apparent.

What I Took Away From This

The interesting part of this project isn't that a portfolio can be generated as static HTML. Static site generation is already a well-established approach.

What I wanted to explore was how much of a conventional content management experience could be retained without introducing the infrastructure that usually comes with it.

By combining GitHub's Contents API, version-controlled configuration, Zod schemas, browser-based editing, and GitHub Actions, I ended up with a system that has:

  • No custom backend to deploy or maintain.

  • No separately hosted database.

  • No server-side runtime requirement for the public website.

  • A browser-based editing experience.

  • Versioned configurations with automatic migrations.

  • Automated image processing.

  • Upstream synchronization for customized forks.

  • Static deployment through GitHub Pages.

There are trade-offs, of course. Editing depends on GitHub, and the current authentication model is designed around an individual maintaining their own repository using a Personal Access Token stored in their browser. It isn't intended to replace a multi-user CMS with role-based access, collaboration, and independent authentication.

But for its intended purpose, I think this is a useful balance.

The project is also something I intend to keep improving. As you will notice if you visit my website, which uses this project, there are always more things to do. More things to refine once a system starts being used beyond its initial implementation. For example, the UI is not the best. I soon want to make this project allow users to choose from several templates. And make it easy to add more if they or any contributors want.

If you'd like to explore the implementation, fork it, or see how the architecture fits together, the repository is available here:

GitHub: nightmaregaurav/portfolio

The idea is straightforward: your portfolio should be about presenting your work, not maintaining the infrastructure required to publish it.
